authors: David Harvey (University of New South Wales, Australia), Joris van der Hoeven (École polytechnique, France)
statement: E. Performing small products in parallel Consider the following problem: given integers u1 , . . . , un and v1 , . . . , vn of bit size p, compute the products u1 v1 , . . . , un vn . Is there a way to reduce this problem to a single integer multiplication problem of size O(np)? (Or O(1) such problems?) We do not know how to do this, but it is not implausible that such a reduction exists. If this reduction were possible, then many of the results of this paper could likely be improved, and the proofs would simplify considerably. Namely, in Theorem 18, the second term l1 l2 n1 n2 M(b) could probably be absorbed into the M(m) term, by performing all the multiplications by Bluestein factors and twiddle factors “in parallel”. This would likely imply that many of the M(m) terms in Section VI could be replaced by simply M(m), which would in turn allow us to strengthen the statements of Theorem 3 and Theorem 4 into more direct lower bounds for M(m).

Is there a way to reduce this problem to a single integer multiplication problem of size O(np)? (Or O(1) such problems?) We do not know how to do this, but it is not implausible that such a reduction exists. If this reduction were possible, then many of the results of this paper could likely be improved, and the proofs would simplify considerably. Namely, in Theorem 18, the second term l1 l2 n1 n2 M(b) could probably be absorbed into the M(m) term, by performing all the multiplications by Bluestein factors and twiddle factors “in parallel”. This would likely imply that many of the M(m) terms in Section VI could be replaced by simply M(m), which would in turn allow us to strengthen the statements of Theorem 3 and Theorem 4 into more direct lower bounds for M(m). A. Alternative complexity models It is interesting to ask what impact our reductions have in complexity models other than the multitape Turing machine. One model often discussed in the context of integer multiplication is the Boolean circuit model [2, §4.3]. The O(n log n) multiplication algorithm of [3] works in this model, and it is reasonable to guess that this is optimal. Unfortunately, matrix transposition is trivial (zero cost!) in this model, so while our reductions still make sense here, they are completely useless. If we want to stay closer to the Turing machine paradigm, one natural variant to consider is the multitape Turing machine with d-dimensional tapes (for fixed d) [9], [28]. While transposition is not free in such a model, it can easily be carried out in linear time (provided that d ⩾ 2), suggesting that our reductions are not especially interesting here either. F. If the conjectured lower bound TT (m) = Ω(m lg m) holds for every binary transposition machine T , then the conjectured lower bound MM (m) = Ω(m lg m) holds for every multiplication machine M . In fact, we can prove something slightly stronger than this: provided that T(m) = ω(m lg lg m), then roughly speaking M(m) = Ω(T(m)), i.e., multiplying integers is at least as hard as transposing matrices of the same bit size. For a precise statement, see Corollary 23. If even the lower bound T(m) = ω(m lg lg m) is out of reach, then we can still say something, but our results are somewhat weaker.
